p.x:
Last week, I felt sick, and I had a terrible pain in my stomach. My body was hot, so my mum used a thermometer. My temperature was 38.5°C! She made an appointment at the clinic near our house.
The doctor was very kind. She listened to my heart and asked me some questions. Then a nurse took some blood from my arm. It didn't hurt much. The doctor said I had a stomach infection and gave me some pills. "Take one pill three times a day," she said. We bought the medicine at the pharmacy next to the clinic.
Three days later, I felt much better. My little brother wasn't so lucky. He fell off his bike and hurt his tooth and his leg. The x-ray showed that a bone in his leg was broken. He didn't need an operation, but he had to wear a bandage for a week, and he needed an injection for the pain.

For thousands of years, diseases like smallpox killed millions of people, and there was no cure. Then, in 1796, an English doctor named Edward Jenner made an important discovery. He noticed that milkmaids who had caught a mild disease from cows did not get smallpox. He created the first vaccine, and over the next two centuries, smallpox was completely removed from the world.
Today, vaccines protect us against many diseases, such as measles and polio. Most are given as an injection, often in the arm. A small dose of a weak or dead germ teaches the body to fight the real disease.
Another great discovery was the antibiotic. In 1928, Alexander Fleming found that a mould could kill bacteria. Antibiotics now treat infections in wounds and organs, helping them heal. Before antibiotics, even a small cut could be deadly.
Modern medicine continues to improve. A surgeon can now replace a damaged heart, and a specialist can treat allergies that once had no treatment. However, doctors warn that we must use medicines carefully and follow their advice.

The COVID-19 pandemic was a reminder that infectious diseases remain one of humanity's greatest threats. Within months of the first outbreak, the virus had spread to almost every country, overwhelming hospitals and disrupting daily life for billions. Yet it also demonstrated the extraordinary speed of modern science: effective vaccines were developed, tested in large clinical trials and approved in less than a year, a process that normally takes a decade.
In a clinical trial, some volunteers receive the real treatment, while others receive a placebo, a substance with no medical effect. Comparing the two groups allows researchers to measure whether the treatment really works. The success of COVID-19 vaccines, which helped millions develop immunity, relied on this careful method.
Experts warn, however, that the next global threat may not be a new virus but an old enemy: bacteria. Through overuse of antibiotics, in both humans and farm animals, many bacteria have become resistant to the drugs designed to kill them. If this continues, routine procedures that require an anaesthetic and a sterile environment, such as a hip replacement or an organ transplant, could become far more dangerous. Some scientists describe this as a 'silent epidemic'.
Meanwhile, other problems require attention. In many countries, there are not enough organ donors to meet demand, and accidental overdoses of common painkillers are rising. Preparing for the future, it seems, requires not only scientific innovation but also responsible behaviour from governments, doctors and patients alike.
